FACT_ID: sec03-F01 | anchor: A23
Clear driving vision helps you read distant signs, judge distances and react to hazards. [A23]
Source: [A23 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec03-F02 | anchor: A23
Have a professional check your eyes every 1 or 2 years and follow the recommendations. [A23]
Source: [A23 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec03-F03 | anchor: A23
Avoid sunglasses and tinted glasses at night because they reduce night vision. [A23]
Source: [A23 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec03-F04 | anchor: A23
Side vision lets you notice vehicles approaching from either side while you look ahead. [A23]
Source: [A23 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec03-F05 | anchor: A23
Clear sight alone does not guarantee accurate distance judgment. [A23]
Source: [A23 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec03-F06 | anchor: A23
Good daytime sight does not guarantee safe vision in dim light or headlight glare. [A23]
Source: [A23 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec03-F07 | anchor: A23
Horns, sirens and tire noise can warn of danger, including a vehicle you cannot see in a blind spot. [A23]
Source: [A23 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec03-F08 | anchor: A23
Drivers with hearing difficulties can compensate by relying more on vision. [A23]
Source: [A23 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec03-F09 | anchor: A23
Keep radio volume low and avoid headsets or earbuds while driving. [A23]
Source: [A23 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec03-F10 | anchor: A23
Fatigue is physical or mental tiredness caused by strain, illness or insufficient sleep. [A23]
Source: [A23 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec03-F11 | anchor: A23
Fatigue can reduce concentration, slow decisions and reactions, and increase irritability. [A23]
Source: [A23 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec03-F12 | anchor: A23
Do not drive when excessively tired because you may fall asleep. [A23]
Source: [A23 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec03-F13 | anchor: A24
Caffeine, loud music and an open window cannot reliably prevent sleep at the wheel. [A24]
Source: [A24 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec03-F14 | anchor: A24
A driver may briefly fall asleep without realizing it; the described microsleeps last 4 to 5 seconds. [A24]
Source: [A24 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec03-F15 | anchor: A24
Only additional sleep repays a sleep debt. [A24]
Source: [A24 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec03-F16 | anchor: A24
Get ample sleep before a trip and plan to drive during your usual waking hours. [A24]
Source: [A24 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec03-F17 | anchor: A24
When you need rest, leave the road and find a safe stopping place rather than pushing on to the destination. [A24]
Source: [A24 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec03-F18 | anchor: A24
The manual advises a safe sleep break during the body’s low-alertness period between midnight and 6 a.m. [A24]
Source: [A24 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec03-F19 | anchor: A24
With a passenger, conversation may help keep the mind engaged, and alternating drivers allows rest. [A24]
Source: [A24 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec03-F20 | anchor: A25
Keep both front-seat occupants awake; a resting driver should buckle up and nap in the rear seat. [A25]
Source: [A25 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F21 | anchor: A25
Plan a driving break every 2 hours or 100 miles, stopping earlier if fatigue warning signs appear. [A25]
Source: [A25 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F22 | anchor: A25
A fatigue refresher nap is described as 15 to 20 minutes. [A25]
Source: [A25 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F23 | anchor: A25
Check medicine labels for drowsiness warnings and avoid alcohol or other drugs when driving. [A25]
Source: [A25 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F24 | anchor: A25
Fatigue warning signs include struggling to keep eyes open, wanting to support the head, repeated yawning, missing memories of recent driving, lane drift and disconnected thoughts. [A25]
Source: [A25 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F25 | anchor: A25
Even a single listed drowsiness warning calls for leaving the road and finding a safe place to nap. [A25]
Source: [A25 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F26 | anchor: A25
A distraction diverts your mind or body from driving. [A25]
Source: [A25 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F27 | anchor: A25
Before departure, switch off phones, set navigation, finish eating or grooming, and secure loose items. [A25]
Source: [A25 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F28 | anchor: A25
While driving, avoid phone conversations, texting, arguments and eating. [A25]
Source: [A25 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F29 | anchor: A25
Secure children with their restraints and keep pets in carriers instead of loose in the vehicle. [A25]
Source: [A25 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec03-F30 | anchor: A26
A visual distraction directs your gaze away from the road toward something unrelated to driving. [A26]
Source: [A26 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F31 | anchor: A26
A manual distraction removes a hand from steering or another driving control for a task unrelated to driving. [A26]
Source: [A26 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F32 | anchor: A26
Cognitive distractions are thoughts or feelings that divert attention from driving. [A26]
Source: [A26 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F33 | anchor: A26
Driving-related checks of instruments, mirrors or installed devices can be safe when each glance lasts less than 1 second and relates only to driving. [A26]
Source: [A26 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F34 | anchor: A27
Pull off the road before dialing a phone number. [A27]
Source: [A27 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F35 | anchor: A27
A passenger can place a phone call so the driver can attend to driving. [A27]
Source: [A27 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F36 | anchor: A27
When reporting an emergency, identify whether medical help or police are needed, give the exact location and report any apparent injuries. [A27]
Source: [A27 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F37 | anchor: A27
Secure a portable phone in its cradle so it does not become a crash projectile. [A27]
Source: [A27 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F38 | anchor: A27
A driver younger than 18 is prohibited from using a mobile phone or handheld electronic device while operating a vehicle, and violating that rule is a traffic infraction. [A27]
Source: [A27 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F39 | anchor: A27
Aggressive driving includes speeding, tailgating, unsafe lane changes, failing to signal turns and disregarding traffic controls. [A27]
Source: [A27 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F40 | anchor: A27
Respond to another driver’s mistake or rudeness with patience and courtesy rather than anger. [A27]
Source: [A27 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F41 | anchor: A28
A driver younger than 21 may not drive after consuming any amount of alcohol. [A28]
Source: [A28 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec03-F42 | anchor: A28
For a driver younger than 21 convicted of OUI, the listed license loss lasts at least 1 year. [A28]
Source: [A28 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec03-F43 | anchor: A28
An underage OUI conviction also brings a fine, a reinstatement fee and a required alcohol-and-drug education, evaluation and treatment program, with jail possible. [A28]
Source: [A28 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec03-F44 | anchor: A28
Alcohol and other impairing drugs can disrupt judgment, vision, color discrimination and reaction time. [A28]
Source: [A28 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec03-F45 | anchor: A28
Do not allow someone who has been drinking to drive. [A28]
Source: [A28 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec03-F46 | anchor: A29
Good judgment means thinking clearly, deciding promptly and assessing time, space and distance. [A29]
Source: [A29 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F47 | anchor: A29
Alcohol impairs judgment, and worsening judgment can accompany further drinking. [A29]
Source: [A29 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F48 | anchor: A29
Alcohol can lengthen recovery from headlight glare and reduce side vision and distance judgment. [A29]
Source: [A29 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F49 | anchor: A29
Alcohol is a depressant that can weaken emotional control and encourage risky decisions. [A29]
Source: [A29 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F50 | anchor: A29
Drinking interferes with concentration, reaction, coordination and alertness, increasing the risk of falling asleep or leaving the road. [A29]
Source: [A29 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F51 | anchor: A29
A drinking driver is more likely to choose an unsuitable speed, pass badly, wander between lanes, miss signals or brake late. [A29]
Source: [A29 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F52 | anchor: A30
Alcohol can create false confidence while sight, reflexes, coordination and judgment deteriorate. [A30]
Source: [A30 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec03-F53 | anchor: A30
The manual’s approximate equal-alcohol servings are 12 ounces of beer, 1 ounce of 100-proof liquor, 4 ounces of table wine or 10 ounces of wine cooler. [A30]
Source: [A30 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec03-F54 | anchor: A30
Intoxication results from drinking too much, rather than merely switching beverage types. [A30]
Source: [A30 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec03-F55 | anchor: A30
Coffee, cold showers and exercise do not sober a drinker; the body needs time. [A30]
Source: [A30 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec03-F56 | anchor: A31
The OUI summary identifies 0.08 grams of alcohol per 100 milliliters of blood or 210 liters of breath as a criminal operating-under-the-influence level. [A31]
Source: [A31 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec03-F57 | anchor: A31
Following arrest, an alcohol-level test result and police report can lead to immediate Secretary of State suspension before court appearance. [A31]
Source: [A31 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec03-F58 | anchor: A31
Breath alcohol concentration is expressed in grams of alcohol per 210 liters of breath and measured by chemical analysis. [A31]
Source: [A31 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec03-F59 | anchor: A31
The amount consumed, elapsed alcohol-elimination time and body weight affect breath alcohol concentration. [A31]
Source: [A31 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec03-F60 | anchor: A31
Alcohol-level testing uses breath or blood samples. [A31]
Source: [A31 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec03-F61 | anchor: A31
The officer normally gives a breath test unless it is judged unreasonable; if no breath test is given, a blood test is required. [A31]
Source: [A31 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec03-F62 | anchor: A31
When a blood test is needed, the driver may choose the physician if that physician is reasonably available. [A31]
Source: [A31 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec03-F63 | anchor: A31
Refusing an implied-consent alcohol test brings immediate administrative license suspension, without needing court action, for up to 6 years. [A31]
Source: [A31 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec03-F64 | anchor: A31
Police testimony about driving performance may support an OUI conviction even without an alcohol-test result. [A31]
Source: [A31 -> pdf-0031]

Misconceptions: feeling more confident after drinking does not establish unimpaired driving. [A30]
Mnemonic: rest, attention, judgment, safe choices.
Glossary: fatigue means physical or mental tiredness. [A23]
Dynamic facts: dated survey figures, cost illustrations and conflicting passenger penalties are held for verification.
